rappel_detail.pull: This is the station where ropes hang up. One party's rope jammed on the pull off the first rappel and had to be freed by hauling on it with a progress-capture pulley. Pull from as far out from the chute as the ledge allows.
rappel_detail.notes: Noticeably shorter than the four rappels below it; the rest of the line runs close to a full 30 m.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing at the true summit, no bolts. What is actually there has changed: a 2018 party found a home-made spinning hanger backed up to a rock pinch, and the local rangers stripped and rebuilt the tat on the lower (west) summit stations that same season because the accumulated slings had become impossible to judge.
hazards: The start is awkward — you squeeze into a narrow chute to get weight onto the rope, which is the least pleasant transition on the descent
Abandoned stations sit further climber's left of the current line and are explicitly not recommended; do not follow old tat leftward
rappel_detail.station: Essentially underfoot once you top out — the flat ground at the true summit. Parties who finish the West Ridge on the lower west summit should not expect an anchor there; at least one party in 2018 found nothing on the west summit and had to continue east to the true summit to start the descent.

rappel_detail.notes: Every station on this line is tat, not fixed hardware; carry cord and be willing to replace rather than add to it.
rappel_detail.anchor: Webbing around a chockstone jammed between the main wall and a protruding flake. Relocated by the climbing rangers in 2018 — it is no longer on the big ledge where it used to be.
hazards: Cramped stance — the relocated station is on a pillar-like perch that is hard to stand at comfortably with two people
Missing it means either climbing back up or committing to unknown ground below
rappel_detail.station: Not visible from the summit. Rappel roughly 25 m and look climber's left. Relative to the old ledge station it sits about 30 ft (9 m) climber's left and about 50 ft (15 m) further down the slope, so parties navigating from a pre-2018 description will rappel straight past where they expect it.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing (tat). No bolts anywhere on this descent.
rappel_detail.station: The one easy station on the line — from station 2 it is in plain sight directly below you.

rappel_detail.pull: Reported as having a great many places for the rope to jam. Flick the strands clear of the alcove and the gully edges before the last climber pulls, and think about which side you pull from.
rappel_detail.notes: After this rappel you can leave the ropes packed and downclimb 3rd class ground climber's right to reach the climbers' trail back to the base of the West Ridge — that scrambling is loose. Optionally, one or two more rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully drop straight onto the climbers’ path instead, rejoining the older rappel line: cleaner ground for more rope work.
hazards: The station sits directly beneath a large volume of loose rock, and getting down from it without knocking anything off is genuinely difficult — keep the rest of the party out from underneath and expect to be hit by what you dislodge yourself
The gully below is broken and full of snag features
Skipping the optional lower stations in favour of the downclimb puts you on loose 3rd class ground with a pack and a rope on your back.
rappel_detail.station: Hidden, and the station people miss. From station 3 you must trend climber's left rather than straight down; it is tucked into a small alcove left of station 3, sitting just above the gully where the ground eases off to 3rd and 4th class.

set.rappels: 4 single-rope rappels down the north side, then a 3rd-class downclimb back toward Prusik Pass; one or two optional extra rappels replace the downclimb.
set.rappel_count_note: Most parties report four rappels on a single 60 m rope, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground to the climbers’ trail; those who count five or six took the optional stations climber’s right of the gully below the fourth instead of downclimbing. A single 60 m rope is adequate at each station for a party of two.
set.descent_text: From the summit, the standard descent drops down the north side of Prusik Peak via a sequence of rappels, then traverses back to Prusik Pass to rejoin the approach line. Most parties make four rappels, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground; one or two optional extra rappels can replace that downclimb - the first anchor is typically right at your feet on a flat spot at/near the true summit, with subsequent stations found by rappelling roughly 20-30m and looking climber's-left; anchors are fixed gear (slings/webbing 'tat' and rap rings/chains left by parties over the years, not bolted), so back them up or inspect carefully. Rappel lengths run mostly in the 25-30m range with one shorter first pitch; a single 60m rope is adequate for every station for a party of two, though a doubled 60m (30m per strand) can feel tight on the last traverse-y rappel, and parties of three often prefer a 70m rope for margin. After the last rappel, traverse west (skiers'-left) across talus back to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge - this is not a walk-off from the summit itself, but the technical descent is short (well under an hour for an efficient party) and feeds directly back into the approach trail. From Prusik Pass, reverse the approach: down into the upper Enchantment Basin, back up and over the rim, then down the loose, steep Aasgard Pass gully to Colchuck Lake (use extra caution here - the scree that makes for a grueling ascent is equally unpleasant and slip-prone descending with tired legs), and out the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead.
